explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. "By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept when we remembered Zion." The captives sat down and the tears came when Jerusalem crossed their minds. I think this is a heart that misses home, and the psalm lets it cry out loud.
Not here, friend. The psalm says "we sat and wept when we remembered Zion." The singing comes up later, and it's not the captives' idea. Right now the only thing flowing by that river is tears.

Close to the mood, but the psalm never mentions fasting. It says "we sat and wept when we remembered Zion." The text gives us tears, plain and simple. I won't add a hunger strike to the story, friend.

explanations.answer: Their captors demanded songs of joy
explanations.explanation: You've got it. "Our captors requested a song; our tormentors demanded songs of joy." The captives were carried off from home, and then the ones holding them wanted a show. I think a harp on a willow branch says plenty about how that felt.

explanations.answer: Their harps had all broken strings
explanations.explanation: Nope, the harps are fine as far as the text tells us. The psalm says "there our captors requested a song; our tormentors demanded songs of joy." The harps hang on the willows because of what was being asked of them. I'd hang mine up too, friend.

explanations.answer: Their leaders told them to stay silent
explanations.explanation: The text goes the other way. It's the captors who ask for songs. "Our tormentors demanded songs of joy: 'Sing us a song of Zion.'" Nobody in this psalm is ordering silence, friend.

Careful, friend, this one's a trap. The captors ask for "a song of Zion," not a song about Babylon. Zion is Jerusalem, the very place the captives were weeping over. Asking them for that song while they're still crying is a lot.
Right. The captors say, "Sing us a song of Zion." Zion is Jerusalem, the home the captives were missing. Nobody asked for a Babylon song. They wanted the one that hit closest to the heart.
Yes, friend. "How can we sing a song of the LORD in a foreign land?" Babylon wasn't home, and the captives felt every mile of it. It's a question, and the psalm leaves it hanging.
Good guess, but barren isn't the word. The psalm says "How can we sing a song of the LORD in a foreign land?" Nothing here says the land was empty or dry. What matters is that it wasn't home.

It sounds right, since the harps are hanging quiet. But the word is "foreign." The psalm asks, "How can we sing a song of the LORD in a foreign land?" The land is foreign, and the captives are the ones going quiet.

That's the one. "If I forget you, O Jerusalem, may my right hand cease to function." The "I" is saying out loud that Jerusalem stays in the heart, no matter how far away it is. It's a promise to remember.
Not quite, friend. The "if" isn't about leaving. The writer says, "If I forget you, O Jerusalem…" It's remembering that's on the line, not the address.
Good thought, but the psalm doesn't say it. The writer says, "If I forget you, O Jerusalem, may my right hand cease to function." The "if" is about forgetting, not about seeing the city again.

True, friend. The writer says, "May my tongue cling to the roof of my mouth if I do not remember you, if I do not exalt Jerusalem as my greatest joy!" Jerusalem is the greatest joy here, even from a far-off land. That's a lot of love for one city.

Other way around, friend. The writer says, "…if I do not exalt Jerusalem as my greatest joy!" So lifting up Jerusalem as the greatest joy is exactly what the writer speaks of. Nothing about it is a maybe.

explanations.answer: Tear it down to its foundations
explanations.explanation: Yes. The sons of Edom said, "Destroy it… tear it down to its foundations!" That's what they were shouting on the day Jerusalem fell. I think that line stuck with the writer, and it comes right out in the prayer.
The psalm doesn't say that. What Edom said was, "Destroy it… tear it down to its foundations!" It's about tearing the city down, not hauling its goods away.
Not in this verse, friend. The sons of Edom said, "Destroy it… tear it down to its foundations!" Their words are about the city itself, right down to its foundations.

Flip it around, friend. The writer says the opposite: "Remember, O LORD, the sons of Edom on the day Jerusalem fell." The prayer asks the LORD to remember, not forget. What Edom said the day Jerusalem fell is right there in the verse.
Correct. The writer prays, "Remember, O LORD, the sons of Edom on the day Jerusalem fell." Remember, not forget. Edom's words are on the writer's mind and brought straight to the LORD.
That's the word. "Blessed is he who repays you as you have done to us." It's a hard line, and it comes from deep hurt. I think this is a writer pouring out pain, and the psalm lets it all show.
You'd think so, but the psalm uses a different word. It says, "Blessed is he who repays you as you have done to us." Blessed, friend, and that's part of what makes this psalm so hard to read.
Not this time. The verse says, "Blessed is he who repays you as you have done to us." The word is blessed, and it's a strong one to hear from a hurting heart.

explanations.answer: As Babylon has done to them
explanations.explanation: Right. "Blessed is he who repays you as you have done to us." The repaying matches what Babylon did. It's a raw, painful cry, and the psalm doesn't soften it.
That would be a whole different psalm, friend. This one says, "Blessed is he who repays you as you have done to us." It's repaying in the same way Babylon did, not with kindness.

explanations.answer: With the riches it once took
explanations.explanation: The psalm doesn't talk about riches here. It says, "Blessed is he who repays you as you have done to us." The repaying is as Babylon has done, and that's all the verse tells us.
